body: EUR/USD 1.1250 (EUR 624.89 mn) 1.1150 (EUR 960.00 mn) USD/JPY 159.00 (US$ 1.65 bn) 158.00 (US$ 4.24 bn) 157.00 (US$ 1.72 bn) GBP/USD 1.3475 (GBP 446.81 mn) 1.3315 (GBP 425.75 mn) 1.3200 (GBP 591.51 mn) USD/CHF 0.8175 (US$ 136.16 mn) 0.8100 (US$ 175.00 mn) USD/CAD 1.4000 (US$ 1.30 bn) 1.3950 (US$ 1.01 bn) AUD/USD 0.6900 (AUD 792.20 mn) 0.6950 (AUD 640.23 mn) NZD/USD 0.5640 (NZD 913.65 mn) What are FX option expiries? The FX option expiration price levels refer to the strike prices where option contracts are set to expire. These levels include both calls and puts. When you see "EUR/USD at 1.1600 for €4 billion" it means there is a total of €4 billion worth of options (calls + puts combined) that have a strike price of 1.1600 and are expiring at that specific time (the "New York Cut" at 10:00 AM ET). Traders watch these levels because they often act as a "magnet" for the price. For example, if there's nothing happening in the market and the price is close to the expiry level, let's say 30-50 pips away, what you will usually see is the price moving into the expiry level. This happens due to the hedging activity of the market makers (banks, dealers and so on). As the price gets closer to the strike price near expiration, these market makers must aggressively buy or sell the currency to hedge their risk. This hedging activity tends to suppress volatility and keep the price "pinned" close to the strike price until the expiration time passes.

The preliminary reading is released at 10 am ET in the first half of each month, based on interviews conducted over the preceding weeks. A final reading incorporating the full sample follows near the end of the month. The preliminary figure sometimes draws a market reaction because it's the first look at the month. The headline Index of Consumer Sentiment is built from questions about personal finances, business conditions and whether it's a good time to buy big-ticket items. It's indexed to 100 in early 1966. The survey splits into two sub-indexes, current economic conditions and consumer expectations. The expectations measure is a component of the Conference Board's Leading Economic Index. Inflation expectations are lately the most market-sensitive part of the release and the Fed will be pleased with the dip in today's report. title: US Used Car Prices Rise in October
body: The Manheim Used Vehicle Value Index rose 0.5% month over month in October 2026, marking its first increase in four months. Prices for non-electric vehicles (non-EVs) were up 0.4%, while electric vehicle (EV) prices declined 0.9%. On a year-over-year basis, used vehicle prices increased 1.9%, reversing a 0.5% decline in the prior month. Gains were led by EVs (up 6.6%) and Compact Cars (up 6.5%), while values for Luxury vehicles (-0.7%), Pickups (-0.7%), and SUVs (-0.2%) continued to edge lower. "October is typically the weakest month of the year, which makes the comparison with last year especially notable. In 2025, the EV tax credit expired in September, temporarily boosting demand for both new and used EVs. Once that support ended, used EV values dropped 3% in October, and non-EV values fell more than 2%, driving steep month-over-month declines in both the index and non-seasonally adjusted prices. This year, both EV and non-EV prices also fell on a non-seasonally adjusted basis, but their declines were far more modest than in 2025," said Jeremy Robb, Chief Economist at Cox Automotive. title: Trump chief of staff Susie Wiles to be replaced by Stephen Miller
body: White House chief of staff Susie Wiles will be leaving her post, President Trump reported. She will move over to the Trump political operation, he said. Her replacement is Stephen Miller, who Trump said is "one of my most trusted advisors". Miller was the deputy chief of staff. Bloomberg reports that Wiles resigned on Thursday night, so this impetus could have come from her, rather than Trump. In any case, Miller is an extreme hawk on immigration and that's what he is best known for. He becamse less prominent after the immigration roundups in Minnesota. Perhaps more importantly, Miller has been one of the most forceful public defenders of Trump's 2026 war against Iran. This could be an early signal that Trump has no plans to make peace or to dial down tariffs. Instead, he may escalate on both fronts in order to re-cast his legacy as someone who made tough choices for the long term. In April, Miller argued that the American blockade could continue indefinitely if Iran refused a deal. He also threatened the potential destruction of Iranian energy infrastructure, although he described that as a last resort. Behind closed doors, there hasn't been much reporting on his stance, so he might just be touting the usual White House talking points. In any case, moving Miller from deputy chief of staff to the top staff position increases his potential influence over which recommendations reach Trump and how decisions are implemented.
